title: Among urban poor respondents, hardship and formative government contact could coincide with political activism
source_unit: 462 low-income men and women in one of the poorest congressional districts in the United States
geography: United States; one poor urban congressional district

observations.period: Study survey; published in Social Problems 48(3), 2001

denominator.unit: low-income men and women surveyed in one poor congressional district

material_resources_and_activism.value: material resources and demographic attributes associated with political activism

severe_hardship_and_participation.value: severe economic hardship associated with greater willingness to participate in the political system

government_contact_and_participation.value: formative contact with government agents associated with greater willingness to participate

observations.method: Survey analysis of low-income residents combining economic hardship, material resources, political attitudes, interactions with government agents, and political activism; the study develops a contextual account of how citizens encounter the political system.
observations.uncertainty: The source is observational and geographically narrow. The abstract does not provide a causal design, complete coefficient table, dated hardship episode, named agency route, or validated later vote. Contact may reflect prior activism, need, institutional exposure, or selection into government interactions.
observations.subgroup: Low-income men and women in one of the poorest congressional districts; not a national representative sample.
observations.counterinterpretation: Hardship and government contact may mobilize grievance or efficacy in some contexts rather than reduce action; the direction can differ from time/resource scarcity findings when the outcome is willingness or activism rather than administrative contact or turnout.

boundary: This record adds an observational hardship-and-government-contact-to-activism surface among low-income urban respondents. It does not establish causality, national prevalence, a specific agency remedy, generalized trust change, validated turnout, or a universal hardship-to-mobilization effect.
